title: China risk returns in American bond markets
gist: The author argues a July 31 joint US-Japan currency intervention conducted in Euros (rather than dollars) reveals the Fed is quietly protecting a fragile Treasury market — where 30-year yields have risen from 1.3% to 5.2% since early 2020 — and that China, having shifted from accumulating Treasuries to building over $1 trillion in 'shadow reserves' at state banks, now has the ability to sell a modest quantity of Treasuries as a low-cost pressure tactic against Washington without depleting its own dollar reserves.

themes.theme: The Yen intervention as a Treasury-market tell

insights.claim: The US and Japan undertook a joint market intervention to prop up a rapidly sliding Yen — an uncommon step outside a crisis, with the last such joint intervention occurring during the 1998 Asian Financial Crisis — but unlike in 1998, when the US sold dollars to buy Yen, this time the New York Fed sold Euro reserves to buy Yen on 31 July.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: The choice to sell Euros rather than dollars for the intervention is the key tell the author uses to argue the Fed was avoiding any dollar-selling pressure that could further strain an already fragile Treasury market — a mechanism worth watching in future currency interventions as a proxy for Treasury-market stress.
insights.locator: Recently when the United States and Japan undertook a joint market intervention

insights.claim: The joint US-Japan statement indicated that for future interventions, Japanese authorities will use the Fed's FIMA (Foreign and International Monetary Authorities) Repo Facility — created during the pandemic to let countries access dollars temporarily using existing US bonds as collateral, without selling their reserves outright.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Signals the Fed is institutionalising a mechanism to prevent allied central banks from having to sell US Treasuries outright to fund currency interventions — a structural workaround worth monitoring as a leading indicator of Treasury-market fragility.

insights.claim: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed the intervention's objective was to avoid Yen weakness spilling over onto other Asian currencies, but mainstream macroeconomic and market consensus disagrees with this framing, instead interpreting the intervention's mechanics as being about protecting the stability of the US Treasury market itself.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: The gap between the official rationale (Asian currency spillover) and market/expert consensus (Treasury market protection) is itself a signal of underlying Treasury market stress that official communications are downplaying.

themes.theme: How fragile the Treasury market has become

insights.claim: Yields on the 10- and 30-year US Treasury bonds have risen sharply since the Iran war, with the 30-year yield up from 1.3% to 5.2% since early 2020, leaving the US government paying its highest borrowing costs on the 10-year bond since 2007 and on the 30-year bond since 2001.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Concrete, severe yield data (30-year up from 1.3% to 5.2% since 2020; highest borrowing costs since 2007/2001) quantifying just how much the US government's financing costs have deteriorated — directly relevant to fiscal sustainability and rate-sensitive asset positioning.
insights.locator: Yields on the 10- and 30-year US bonds have shot up

insights.claim: The author identifies four interconnected structural sources of US Treasury weakness: persistent post-pandemic inflation eroding Fed credibility after five years of missing its 2% target; increasingly unsustainable US debt dynamics; new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh being caught between presidential pressure to cut rates and market conditions that prevent it, producing muddled rhetoric that further erodes Fed credibility; and a structural shift of global capital flows away from government bonds toward US equities and corporate debt.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: A four-factor diagnostic framework for Treasury market weakness (inflation credibility, debt sustainability, Fed leadership credibility, capital-flow reallocation to equities/corporate debt) useful for ongoing US rates and fiscal-risk analysis.
insights.locator: To answer that, we must first look at the sources of weakness

insights.claim: Global capital increasingly flows into US equities and corporate debt rather than government debt, a structural shift that is undermining the dollar's 'exorbitant privilege' as global reserve currency, since Treasuries now must compete with equity markets for money.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural (not cyclical) shift in global capital allocation away from Treasuries toward US equities/corporate debt — a long-term thesis relevant to positioning across the Treasury-vs-equity allocation debate.

themes.theme: China's shift from Treasuries to 'shadow reserves'

insights.claim: Since around 2015, as Beijing stopped accumulating more dollars in its official foreign reserves, that accumulation shifted to China's state-run commercial banks; China's publicly disclosed $1.8 trillion forex reserves have stayed almost flat for a decade even as Chinese banks now hold over $1 trillion in what the author calls 'shadow reserves.'
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Reveals that China's true dollar-asset exposure is understated by its official $1.8 trillion reserve figure by over $1 trillion held opaquely in state banks — a material data point for anyone modelling China's actual dollar exposure and de-dollarization narrative.

insights.claim: China's trade surplus, now over $1 trillion, needs to be parked somewhere, and the dollar being the safest financial asset is effectively the only real choice — even as China's holdings of US Treasuries specifically have fallen from $1.2 trillion to around $650 billion over the past decade.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Quantifies China's roughly 46% reduction in Treasury holdings ($1.2tn to ~$650bn) over a decade even as its trade surplus and total dollar exposure kept growing — direct evidence of a deliberate portfolio shift away from Treasuries specifically, not away from dollars generally.

themes.theme: China's new Treasury-market leverage over the US

insights.claim: As China's exposure to Treasuries falls, it gains the ability to operationalise its remaining holdings as a soft weapon: during a future tense episode with the US, Beijing could sell a modest quantity of American bonds to hike Treasury yields and raise an already heavily indebted country's borrowing costs, a tactic likely to spook any US administration.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Central actionable thesis: China's reduced Treasury exposure paradoxically increases its coercive leverage over US borrowing costs, since a modest sale now has outsized proportional impact — a geopolitical risk factor for US rates markets during any future US-China confrontation.
insights.quote: China doesn't have to tank the US bond market, just hike it up a little bit to make Washington concede on a given day.
insights.locator: China doesn't have to tank the US bond market

insights.claim: Historically China was unlikely to dump US Treasuries because doing so would erode the value of its own foreign exchange reserves, which it relied on to manage its currency; today, however, China holds ample dollars via its shadow reserves and is far less dependent on Treasuries specifically for currency management, removing that historical deterrent.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Explains the mechanism by which China's old self-deterrent against selling Treasuries (fear of devaluing its own reserves) has weakened — a structural change in the US-China financial 'balance of terror' that increases the plausibility of China using Treasury sales as leverage.

insights.claim: The shift from holding Treasuries to holding cash dollars in shadow reserves has given China a subtle new source of financial leverage over Washington, with Beijing now able to pressure the US by hiking Treasury rates at will, without touching its much larger stock of dollar reserves.
insights.speaker: Srijan Shukla
insights.so_what: Summarizes the article's core geopolitical-financial risk thesis: monitor China's Treasury holdings and any sudden sales as a potential coercive signal during US-China tensions, distinct from broader de-dollarization narratives.
insights.quote: The shift from bonds to cash dollars has given China a subtle source of leverage.
